extracted.intended_audience: administrative law practitioners, trade lawyers, agency officials, and judges handling APA rulemaking and antidumping disputes
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria governing (1) when agencies must use notice-and-comment rulemaking to promulgate, amend, or repeal regulations, (2) when exceptions (good cause / harmless error) apply, and (3) statutory/agency standards for applying antidumping methodologies (targeted dumping / average-to-transaction).

rubrics_metrics.name: APA notice-and-comment requirement for rulemaking (including repeal/withdrawal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever an agency decides to 'formulat[e], amend[], or repeal[] a rule,' it must first publish a notice of proposed rulemaking setting forth 'either the terms or substance of the proposed rule[,] or a description of the subjects and issues involved.' For the purposes of notice and comment, withdrawal or repeal of an existing regulation is treated the same as promulgation of a new regulation. Adequate notice 'must be sufficient to fairly apprise interested parties of the issues involved.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: (a) withdrawal/repeal triggers the same APA §553(b) requirements as a new rule; (b) the notice need not specify every precise proposal but must fairly apprise interested parties so they can provide meaningful comment; (c) adequate notice ensures diverse public comment, fairness, and opportunity to develop record evidence to support objections. (Citations and examples in text: 5 U.S.C. §§ 553(b), 551(5); Nuvio Corp.; Int’l Union v. MSHA.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical outgrowth doctrine for adequacy of notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The dispositive question is whether an agency's final rule is a 'logical outgrowth' of an earlier request for comment: a final rule is a logical outgrowth only if interested parties should have anticipated that the change was possible and reasonably should have filed their comments during the notice-and-comment period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency notices that 'expressly asked for comments on a particular issue' or made clear the contemplated change tend to satisfy the doctrine. Limits: a final rule has to 'find roots' in the proposal; 'something is not a logical outgrowth of nothing.' Courts balance adequate notice values with the public interest in expedition and finality. (Cases: Long Island Care, CSX, Kooritzky, Envtl. Integrity Project.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity required in NPRM to permit radical changes (no 'hintless' switches)
rubrics_metrics.description: An NPRM must contain enough specificity that an 'interested person' could have perceived the possibility of the agency's ultimate action; where the notice gives no hint (the 'merest hint' absent), the final action is not a logical outgrowth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative failure: Kooritzky—notice contained 'nothing, not the merest hint' that the agency might tighten practice; result invalidated. Mere mention of a related subject without clear indication that repeal or a wholesale change is under consideration is inadequate (see CSX analogy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on bootstrapping notice from public comments
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency generally 'cannot bootstrap notice from a comment'—the existence of comments advocating a change does not cure an NPRM that failed to give fair notice of that change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments interpreting the existing regulation more broadly or narrowly do not substitute for a proper NPRM that proposes repeal or a materially different rule; where commenters did not perceive repeal as an issue, that supports finding inadequate notice (Fertilizer Inst.; Council Tree Commc’ns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good cause exception to notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA's good cause exception permits an agency to forgo notice-and-comment where notice is 'impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest'; agency must show why prior notice and opportunity for comment are impracticable and contrary to public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts scrutinize good-cause invocations strictly. Typical permissible grounds include genuine exigency (e.g., short statutory deadlines to implement complex schemes). Mere administrative convenience or theoretical urgency, or asserted pocketbook/economic harms to regulated entities, generally do not justify good cause. An agency cannot later invent new justifications unsupported in the original notice. (Cited authorities and examples: Mack Trucks, Council of S. Mountains, Gold East Paper.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal exigency and narrowness of good-cause claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To invoke good cause the agency must show a real, concrete urgency—e.g., a true need to act immediately because of statutory or administrative deadlines or risk of serious harm to public interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An alleged need because the regulation applied to ongoing investigations is not necessarily sufficient if the claimed exigency is theoretical (e.g., agency did not apply the withdrawal for months). Courts will examine whether the claimed urgency was factual and contemporaneous and whether less drastic steps were available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmless error analysis for procedural rulemaking defects
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency violates APA procedural requirements, courts consider whether the error was harmless by evaluating prejudice and the nature of the procedural failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish 'technical failure' (some notice given; challenger must show they would have submitted additional/different comments that could have altered the outcome) from 'complete failure' (total absence of notice-and-comment; even minimal uncertainty precludes harmlessness). Prejudice in some contexts means injury to the interests the statute/regulation is designed to protect, but courts also consider whether the procedural omission could have affected the substantive result. (Cited: United States v. Reynolds; Riverbend Farms; Intercargo.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prejudice standard under harmless-error rubric
rubrics_metrics.description: For technical failures challengers may need to show that, had proper notice been provided, they would have submitted additional/different comments that could have invalidated the rationale; in 'complete failure' cases, uncertainty as to effect of failure typically defeats harmless-error defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intercargo indicates prejudice is not shown merely because a party lost on the merits; prejudice is harm to the interests rulemaking was meant to protect. But where the record is thin and agency did not engage issues, courts are unlikely to deem the procedural lapse harmless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory prerequisites for applying average-to-transaction dumping methodology (Tariff Act §1677f-1(d)(1)(B))
rubrics_metrics.description: Commerce may use the average-to-transaction methodology only if: (1) it finds 'a pattern of export prices (or constructed export prices) for comparable merchandise that differ significantly among purchasers, regions, or periods of time' (i.e., targeted dumping); and (2) it explains 'why such differences cannot be taken into account using' the average-to-average or transaction-to-transaction methodologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both predicate findings are required before the average-to-transaction method is available; courts have required explanations why the other statutory methods fail to account for the price differences (see U.S. Steel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting Regulation standard (19 C.F.R. § 351.414(f)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Limiting Regulation provided that even where statutory criteria for average-to-transaction are met, Commerce would 'normally limit the application of the average-to-transaction method to those sales that constitute targeted dumping,' rather than applying it to all of a respondent’s sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation functions as a default/normal rule: application to all sales is not the norm and must be justified. Repeal of such a limiting regulation requires APA compliance; applying the regulation on remand must be consistent with its language and may not be overturned absent clear error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nails (two-part) targeted-dumping test (proposed methodology described)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commerce's proposed two-part 'Nails' test: (1) determine the share of the allegedly targeted customer's purchases (by value) at prices more than one standard deviation below the weighted-average price to all customers; if that share exceeds 33% of exporter’s sales to that customer, the pattern requirement is met; (2) determine whether the share of sales for which the difference between the targeted customer's sales-weighted average and the next higher non-targeted customer exceeds the average price gap for the non-targeted group exceeds 5% of total sales value—if so, the price differences are 'significant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an example of a statistical test Commerce proposed for identifying targeted dumping; the Proposed Methodology sought comments on this test and related issues including whether and when to apply average-to-transaction to all sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zeroing practice in margin calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically Commerce used 'zeroing' in average-to-transaction calculations: negative dumping margins (sales above normal value) are assigned a value of zero and only positive margins are aggregated, so negative margins do not offset positive ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zeroing leads to higher dumping margins and has been controversial; the practice is an important factor when agencies choose among methodologies because use/nonuse of zeroing affects outcomes and agencies must account for its effects in rulemaking/decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of judicial review of agency action (substantial evidence / arbitrary-and-capricious)
rubrics_metrics.description: A court will affirm an agency action unless it is 'unsupported by substantial evidence on the record' or 'otherwise not in accordance with law.' Additionally, agency decisions will be set aside if arbitrary and capricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For APA statutory interpretation questions courts review de novo rather than deferring to the agency; however, for interpretation of ambiguous statutes generally Chevron deference may apply if the agency followed proper procedures and offered reasoned explanation. Auer (or Seminole Rock) governs deference to agency interpretation of its own regulations, but courts will not defer where the agency's application is plainly erroneous or inconsistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on post hoc rationalizations and new justifications
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may not rely on new justifications not presented in the original notice to justify bypassing APA procedures (e.g., invoking a different 'good cause' theory on appeal that was not in Withdrawal Notice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require that the agency's explanation for dispensing with notice-and-comment appear in the rulemaking record; later-invented rationales cannot validate a prior procedural default (N.C. Growers and related authority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of agency response to comments and reference to prior notices in assessing adequacy of notice
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency that withdraws a regulation should typically refer to prior notices and respond to comments; failure to reference or respond to prior notices/comments undermines the conclusion that adequate notice and opportunity for comment were provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of citation to prior NPRMs or lack of response to comments supports finding that withdrawal was not a logical outgrowth of prior notices; courts consider whether the agency engaged substantively with the comments it received when evaluating notice adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remand application and deference to agency's reasonable application of its own regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: On remand, a court will not displace an agency's reasoned application of its own rule unless the agency's interpretation contravenes an unambiguous statutory provision or is plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the agency applies the Limiting Regulation in a reasoned way and the challenger does not show the application is arbitrary, capricious, or contrary to unambiguous statute, courts will defer to the agency's judgment (Auer / Seminole Rock principles cited).
